title: Morton's royalties and Russell's Morton album in California
summary: Morton's lawsuits over royalties, Russell reviewing the Morton album, Dave Stewart, and rumours about Morton in Los Angeles.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: He was dead in that two summer.

Well, yeah, the next summer, that was the fall of 1940, and he died in June. But he was talking how at that time he was still going to sue either MCA or he was suing ASCAP. He was always suing somebody for a million dollars, not paying royalties on his tunes. I mean, he had big ideas like that, exaggerated some things of that kind of, he wouldn't have been due a million dollars royalty, but he figured a lot of people were cashing in on his work, which they did. They never got to be millionaires, of course, but still they did, he didn't get much royalty. I don't doubt for a minute that he didn't get his full royalties out of his publications, but he was all excited about that. I was trying to tell him a few of his old friends I'd seen in California, people he played with, Howard, not Darnell Howard, but the other sax player out there who had a band, I can't think of his name, and a few other people, he thought they were great, in fact, he always had words of praise for almost everybody. Howard, he thought was about the best sax player, I can't think, Dick Allen would know his name instantly, I can't think, he's made a couple of records out there, with, not extra good, but a medium sized band, not a really big band. And other people, speaking of California, when I was out there, I tried to collect some information on Jelly, because his general album, the beautiful one that came out on Commodore later, had just come out, and Charles Smith knew that that time that the average reviewer in any music magazine would pan the thing, although surprising, a downbeat that time did give one of his vocals on, I believe, Mamie's Blues, that was one of the two or three outstanding vocals of the year, in blues vocals, they did like that. So Charles had supervised and arranged the sessions, so he arranged with this tempo magazine that I review the album. But even then, I'm not trying to knock Dave Stewart, he's a wonderful guy and a good friend, I mentioned that Dave came down and recorded Bunk for the first time at all, but I took that album around, I didn't have a phonograph, I had to take it over to Dave's shop to play, and whenever customers would come in, Dave would say, you better not play that, you might drive some of the customers away. And a year later when Jelly came out there, Dave got so crazy about Jelly that he was the only one that went to Jelly's funeral, and he was writing a book, I was starting to take down in longhand a dictation that book for Jelly, only got a couple of pages before Jelly got sick. So he was certainly the number one Jelly fan, but the year before when I brought that general album out, he said, don't play it in the store, when people are here, they chase out the customers. So you can see why Charles did want me to review it because he knew I liked Jelly. But anyway, I ran all over the town trying to find people that knew Jelly and dug up a few pictures at the barber shop, I believe Sutherland or somebody had a trombone player who played in the black and tan. People out there, some of those musicians didn't like Jelly because he was better than they were. As Minette will tell too, when the Ori's band went out, they had a lot of trouble, they'd try to chase him out of town. They'd have prohibition agents to rate him and all too because the fellas out there couldn't play that New Orleans style same way Chicago. They were getting all the work and all the crowds going. But I know one fella said that Jelly didn't get all those diamonds all just for music. They implied he was either a procurer or a pimp, you know. And possibly he had been mixed up in all the district. He might have been mixed up in some of the prostitution racket out there too, which I don't know that there's any evidence to that. But I mean they said that's where he got all of his diamonds and his money and his Cadillacs and so on or whatever he had.
